lesson.title: From Workshops to Empires: Why Big Business Took Over
lesson.summary: In the decades after the Civil War, a combination of abundant resources, new technology, cheap labor, expanding railroads, and a government reluctant to interfere allowed American businesses to grow to a scale never before seen.
lesson.body:
Between the end of the Civil War in 1865 and the turn of the twentieth century, the United States transformed from a mostly agricultural nation into the world's leading industrial power. Several forces converged to make this possible. The country possessed vast natural resources, including coal in Pennsylvania and West Virginia, iron ore around the Great Lakes, and later oil in Pennsylvania and Ohio. It also had a rapidly growing workforce, fed by high birth rates and by waves of immigrants arriving from Europe who were willing to work in mines, mills, and factories for low wages. Neither resource nor labor alone would have mattered without a way to move materials and goods across the country, which is exactly what railroad expansion provided, connecting mines, farms, factories, and cities into a single national market for the first time.

New technology multiplied what workers and machines could produce. Innovations like the Bessemer process for making steel cheaply and quickly, along with new machine tools and factory organization, let companies produce goods on a scale that would have been unimaginable a generation earlier. At the same time, the corporation as a legal form matured, allowing businesses to raise huge amounts of capital by selling stock to many investors while limiting each investor's personal financial risk. This let ambitious entrepreneurs assemble far more money than any individual or partnership could have provided on its own.

Government policy generally encouraged this growth rather than restraining it. Protective tariffs shielded American manufacturers from foreign competition, and lawmakers at the federal, state, and local level mostly followed a laissez faire philosophy, a belief that government should interfere as little as possible in the economy. Courts frequently sided with businesses in labor disputes, and there was little regulation of working conditions, wages, or business consolidation. This hands off environment let successful firms grow largely unchecked.

The result was the emergence of enormous companies concentrated in industries like steel, oil, and railroads, run by a small number of ambitious business leaders who built empires within a single working lifetime. These figures, who would soon be labeled both captains of industry and robber barons depending on one's view of their methods, used strategies like horizontal integration and vertical integration to dominate their markets and often organized their companies into trusts to control prices and eliminate competition.

The rise of big business changed American life far beyond the factory floor. It created enormous new fortunes and a visible class of wealthy industrialists, while also drawing millions of workers into crowded industrial cities where wages were low and conditions were often dangerous. It reshaped politics, as business leaders gained influence over lawmakers, and it triggered new debates over whether the freedom to build a business empire should have any limits, debates that would eventually produce laws like the Sherman Antitrust Act.
